utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed the ... Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. I was informed that the Prosecution would like to address the Chamber. Mr. Dutertre, is it you? Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, thank you. I wanted to provide some explanations as regards the 68 document; i.e., the six documents that were provided yesterday by the Defence team of Mr. Haradinaj. Some research has been carried out - they're actually still underway - in order to better understand the situation. However, I can already indicate that document number 1, which of course is a list of policemen, Serb policemen, with an ID number K0111310 up to 1322 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dutertre, I think that we agreed that any questioning on this material, we would be provisionally in private session. Of course, if you now start explaining what this material is all about, then we would miss the effect of private session later on. So, therefore, I suggest to you that you request for private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. D8, D9, D10, and D11 have been marked for identification. These are signature by Witness 19, ICTY witness statement of Witness 19, 18th of July and 20th of October, 2004. D10, ICTY witness statement of Witness 19, 24th and 26th of July, 2006; D11, ICTY witness statement of Witness 19, on the 9th of October, 2005. Are you going to tender these documents in evidence or not? Because we'd like to know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is not my intention to tender the witness statements into evidence. It is my intention to tender what I believe is D8, which is the signature page of the witness, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's the page with three signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then D8, any objection against admission into evidence, Mr. Di Fazio? Mr. Dutertre? MR. DI FAZIO: No, there's certainly no objection to that, the signature being put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then D8 will be admitted. MR. DI FAZIO: But the other documents, if Your Honours please, the statements may cause some problems further down the line. If Your Honours will want to at some point evaluate what the witness said and contrast it with what is in his statements at some point, at some later point, how will you do that if it's not in evidence? That's the point I raise, and it's a matter for the Trial Chamber. In certain jurisdictions, my application would be to you to say, Well, he's cross-examined on them; they have to go in. But I just raise that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, to the extent the witness is cross-examined on them, the relevant portion has been put to him and has been read to him, so to that extent, on the specific issues on which he was cross-examined, we have it; and what he has seen and what signatures we have seen becomes clear from D8. So, therefore, at this moment -- and, of course, it might not be fair to start seeking consistency or inconsistency apart from where the witness has testified in court. Therefore, it would be a kind of an exercise where the parties would not be aware what we would be focusing on. So for the time being, the Chamber ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the time being, Mr. Di Fazio and Mr. Guy-Smith, the Chamber does not insist on having the statements themselves, that's D9, D10, and D11, into evidence. If, however, there would ever be a moment where the Chamber considers it necessary to call this evidence in whatever circumstances, with or without further testimony of the witness, then, of course, the parties will be informed about it. But the Chamber has the power to order certain material to be adduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour will recall there was one passage in the statement of Witness 19 that I invited him to read to himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then asked him some questions about it, and I think Your Honour asked me at that point did I want to make the statement an exhibit, and I said no. My understanding was that it having been marked for identification, there would be a hyperlink on the transcript which enables that passage to be checked, if needs be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the time being, we leave it as it is. Again, as I said before, if the Chamber at any stage considers it necessary to have a closer look at it and to consider it also in the preparation of the determinations the Chamber will have to make, we'll announce that, parties will have an opportunity to comment on it, and then a decision will be taken. But for the time being, they're just marked for identification. Then is there any other matter? If not, I'd like to give you an opportunity to -- Mr. Emmerson, to continue your cross-examination, and I invite Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. I'm unequally treating the Prosecution because P22 still is on my list. That's the terrorist report regarding terrorist attack on the 2nd of March. Is that tendered? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection? Then P22 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vlahovic. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Emmerson will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Emmerson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, I was asking you yesterday afternoon some questions about conversations you had with people about your parents between April and the end of August, beginning of September, and I told you I was going to come back later to conversations that you'd had, or say you'd had, with people in September. There is one conversation that is recorded in your witness statement, or one piece of information, I should say, that is recorded in your witness statement that you said you had received about your parents which was not mentioned in your evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And for the record, it's page 5, first paragraph, of Mr. Vlahovic's April 2002 witness statement. I don't ask for it to be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to read you the paragraph. You are recorded as having said: "On or around the 10th of May, I heard a false rumour from Nuo Alakaj," A-l-a-k-a-j, "a Catholic from Marnule" M-a-r-n-u-l-e, "Gjakova municipality, to the effect that my parents had been released. Nuo said that he had heard that my parents had been released at Prilep. Nuo told me he had heard this from Zef," Z-e-f, "Hiseni," H-i-s-e-n-i, "from Donji Ratis"? Now, first of all, is that right? Did you hear a false rumour from Nuo Alakaj that your parents had been released at Prilep?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Nuo told me and he had heard this from Zef, from Donji Ratis.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So did Nuo tell you that himself?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with Nuo or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That was what I wanted to ask you. So your brother talked to Nuo and your brother Rade told you what Nuo had said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And what Rade told you was that Nuo had told him that your parents had been released alive at Prilep; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's what he said, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to put to you a passage of Rade's witness statement, please, and ask you to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And this is paragraph 39 and 40 of Mr. Rade Vlahovic's witness statement of the 30th of June, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In that statement, your brother is recorded as having said: "In May 1998 I heard from Catholic Albanian friends from Djakovica that they had learned from relatives in Gornji Ratis that my parents had been taken by Ramush Haradinaj's men to the KLA HQ in Glodjane. The names of these Catholic Albanian friends are Nuo Alakaj and Cuo Alakaj. They are still living in the village of Marnule near Djakovica." That is the passage I want to put to you. So in Rade Vlahovic's statement, he was saying that Nuo Alakaj had told him that your parents had been taken by Ramush Haradinaj's men to Gllogjan, but you're telling us, are you, that what he told you Nuo Alakaj had said was that your parents had been released alive in Prilep.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently that's what Zef from Donji Ratis had told him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move closer to the microphone and speak up, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I suppose that was true. Had it not been true, I don't think that would come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what that answer means, Mr. Vlahovic, but let me just be clear with you. You've told us just a moment ago that what Rade told you Nuo Alakaj had told him was that your parents had been released alive at Prilep. That's what he told you Nuo Alakaj had told him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he told me that he had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And he'd heard it from Nuo Alakaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Rade joined the police, the MUP, in 1990, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And he was a serving police officer throughout the 1990s and throughout 1998 and 1997, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And throughout 1999 as well?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know what the initials PJP stand for, Mr. Vlahovic, in the police context?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: My pronunciation will probably be at fault, but Posebne, P-o-s-e-b-n-e, Jedinice, J-e-d-i-n-i-c-e, Policije, P-o-l-i-c-i-j-e. Have you heard of that branch of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's the PJP, Mr. Vlahovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They're paramilitary police, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. How am I supposed to know? That's beyond my area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your brother Rade was a member of the PJP, was he not, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. We have official records, Mr. Vlahovic, that show that in March 1999, Rade was a member of the paramilitary police? And are you telling us you didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How am I supposed to know that? I wasn't working in the police. I didn't know who worked where, and I never asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you see him in uniform in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, March 1999 was the question, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the same uniform like everybody else. I didn't see any special uniform on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you never saw him carrying an AK-47 automatic rifle, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody had the same uniform at the time, and I may have seen someone carrying an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know the name Mundza, a paramilitary group within the PJP?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You've never heard of the Mundza, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Rade Markovic and Zvonko Markovic, you told us that they were your cousins in the sense that your father and their mother were brother and sister; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My mother and their father were brother and sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. And you told us in your evidence yesterday that you saw them frequently at this time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Both of them were members of the MUP reserve, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever see them in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see many people in uniforms. All those who were in the police were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm asking you about your cousins, Mr. Vlahovic. Did you ever see them in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What year are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Any time in 1998 or 1999. Did you see them in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I'm not sure whether it was 1998 or 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Rade Markovic used to carry an AK-47 when he was in uniform. Did you ever see him with that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify for me what an AK-47 is?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You don't know what an AK-47 is, Mr. Vlahovic? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Is that an automatic rifle? I've never heard that designation, "AK-47?"

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is an automatic rifle. Did you ever see your cousin Rade with an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the other Markovic family? Branislav and Slavisa, were either of them at any time, any time at all, in the MUP reserve?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't know, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about your immediate family. You've told us you yourself before never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, just for me not to be confused, when you're talking about Branislav and Slavisa, let me just see --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to remind Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There were two Markovic families in this witness's evidence. One was escorted out of Dashinoc by Djevdet Sadikaj. They are relatives, but distant relatives, of the other branch of the Markovic family. The two I put the witness -- put to the witness a moment ago, Rade Markovic and Zvonko Markovic, are the immediate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The full cousins. I'm just -- Yes. Branislav and Slavisa, is that where the father had died --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and where Milojka was the mother?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. I've got the right people in mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you were never in the MUP at any time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You yourself, you were never in the MUP at any time?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I ask you this - and do be careful with your answers, if you will - did you ever wear a uniform during 1998 or 1999, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever carry a gun?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a hunting carbine with a licence, and I had a licensed pistol as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What was the pistol for?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had it. I had a licence for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What did you use it for?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't carry it and I didn't use it. You asked me if I had one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Why did you have one, Mr. Vlahovic? It wasn't for hunting, was it? You don't hunt with a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept it at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What about your brother -- I'm sorry, were you going to say something?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say, was that something bad, that I had a pistol?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's not for me to comment, Mr. Vlahovic. What about your brother Novak? Was he ever in the MUP at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And when was he in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the reserve during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was he in the reserve during 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you see him in uniform and carrying a gun?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: An automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What about your brother Goran?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What about my brother Goran? I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Same question I'm asking you. I'm going to ask you about a number of people, so this question I'm asking you about each of them is, were they, to your knowledge, ever in the MUP or the MUP reserve; did they, to your knowledge, ever wear a uniform; and did they, to your knowledge, ever carry a weapon; and if so, what weapon? Those are the questions I'm asking you. Now, what about Goran?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was in the reserve, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you see him in uniform and with a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably I did. I wasn't paying attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So do I have it right that of the four brothers, you're the only one who wasn't in the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Okay. Tell me about the Stojanovic brothers. Any of them in the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let's go through them. Predrag, was he in the police?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, interpreter's correct: The witness said no instead of yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what that was a "no" to, so perhaps we can just put the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Were any of them were in the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Are you saying none of them were in the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's be clear. Let's go through them one at a time. Predrag, you knew him well, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him but not well. He was my senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was he in the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that he was in the PJP serving alongside your brother Rade, Mr. Vlahovic. You did know that he was in the PJP, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know. How could I have known? Was I supposed to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What about Vesko? Do be careful with your answers, Mr. Vlahovic. What about Vesko? Was he in the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think he was. I didn't have all the information who was in the police or not. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that as a school teacher in the area, you knew all these families well. You were able to give us all of their family relationships, Mr. Vlahovic. Let's be frank about this. Did you or did you not know whether Dragoslav Stojanovic was in the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, and I still don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What about Stanisa Radosevic? He's someone you told us you knew well. Stanisa Radosevic, was he in the police at this time during 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he started working in late 1999 or in the year 2000, but I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, in March 1999, Stanisa Radosevic was working with your brother in the PJP, wasn't he, your brother Rade, in the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know who he was working with. I just know that he joined later, rather late, but I don't know who he was working with.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right. You're giving firm evidence about this, Mr. Vlahovic. Your evidence is that he joined late. When you say "late," let's be clear. When do you say -- since you know him obviously well enough to know when he joined, you tell us when he joined the police?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he joined at a later stage. That's what I said. But who he was working with and what he was doing, I don't know, and I don't know when things happened exactly. I wasn't interested in memorising dates and years, and I wasn't privy to how the police operated and who was a member. So I cannot answer any of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You told us he started working late 1999 or in the year 2000. Now, is it your evidence that Stanisa Radosevic was not in the police during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have been a member before that. I don't know. I don't know when he started and when he was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Why, if you don't know, did you tell us just a moment ago that he started working in late 1999 or the year 2000? Why did you say that? MR. DI FAZIO: I object to that. That was immediately followed, if you read the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. MR. DI FAZIO: -- if you read the line, that he said immediately following after 2000, "I don't know." It's in the very line. "I believe that he started working in late 1999 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said "I believe he started working in late 1999 or in the year 2000, but I'm not sure, I don't know." MR. DI FAZIO: "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just a couple lines further down: "I don't know. I don't know who he was working with. I just know that he joined later, rather late ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you then perhaps limit your question to late --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can move on. I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What about Radoje Radosevic, his brother?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Konstantin Stijovic's sons, Novak and Momo. What about them?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't in Decani in 1999. How can I know who was working and where? I know that before that they weren't working, but whether they were working during the war or not, how can I know? I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Simple question: Did you ever see either of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just to be clear, are you saying you don't know one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I wonder if you could just be shown a list, please, single sheet of paper, on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- we're still in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm happy -- I think the matter has been dealt with, with this witness. I'm not going to traverse it necessarily in the same detail with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any -- is it just in order to have the names written down or is there -- do you want to tender that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I will tender the document, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it needs a number. Madam Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number D14, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vlahovic, this is a list of names who are shown in the records of the PJP as having been in receipt of salaries from the PJP in March 1999, and I just want to go through the list. The first one, obviously, is your brother; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put the question clearly, Mr. Emmerson? It's unclear whether it's right that this is his brother or whether it's right that he was in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You told us already your brother was in the police force. That is your brother's name, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Stanisa Radosevic, did you know more than one Stanisa Radosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I knew just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Zeljko Radosevic. Now, you told us yesterday that you don't know that man; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What about Slobodan Markovic? Is that a name you know? No?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Momcilo Markovic. You don't know that man?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Danilo Stijovic, you told us yesterday, was a cousin of the Momo Stijovic who had been injured in Gllogjan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Momo was wounded, but Danilo, I didn't know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. You told us yesterday that he was the cousin, Danilo was the cousin, of the Momo Stijovic who was injured in Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. Momo was the one who was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And Danilo was his cousin; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were related. I'm not sure how distantly. I didn't know him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you did know them both, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. You know how it was, just superficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And Predrag Stojanovic, that's the son of Ljubica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably. Ljubica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Veselin Stojanovic. Is that Vesko?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not, but I don't know. Vesko is probably his real name but I'm not sure. I don't believe this would be him. I think not but I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. But you know who Ljubisa Radunovic is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I do. Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He's the son of Milos and Milka Radunovic, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milica Radunovic, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, were you aware that your brother Rade was involved in the investigation into the late Radonjic Canal find, in his capacity as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. How could he have been involved in that investigation? I don't know about that at all. I don't think he could possibly have been involved in an investigation like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, he was involved in that investigation, Mr. Vlahovic. Did he not tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He didn't tell me and I'm not clear how he possibly could have been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he not tell you that he interviewed a number of Albanians in custody about the canal? Did he not tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked him to begin with. We didn't discuss that, not ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Not even after it was discovered that one of your parent's bodies had been found there? He never told you, I've interviewed people about this canal?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never asked him after about the canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You wouldn't ask him if you didn't know, would you? The question I'm asking you is: Is it right that he never volunteered that information to you, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never said and I never asked. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What about your cousin Zvonko Markovic? Is he someone that you've told us you saw regularly at this time. Did you know that he took part in the recovery operation at the canal? Sorry, let me ask the question again. You told us yesterday you saw your cousin Zvonko Markovic frequently at this time. Did he tell you that he was involved in the recovery operation at the Lake Radonjic Canal?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say. I went there myself and I saw the bodies. I don't know who was involved. I never asked if anybody was involved or not, because I saw the bodies myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you see your cousin there, Zvonko, in uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was there I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And he never told you that he was involved in that part of the operation?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked; he never said.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Similarly about Dashinoc, did he tell you that he had been to Dashinoc, to the site where it is said that the bodies of Milos Radunovic and Slobodan Radosevic were found? Did he tell you that he was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask. I went there myself as well. Why would I have asked him? I'd been there myself. I'd been to both places. That's why I never bothered to ask him about either place.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Well, let's just look at the time that you went there, then, Mr. Vlahovic. You've told us about two conversations that you had in September after the Serbs took control of the area around Ratishe in Dashinoc, one with someone called Shaban Sadikaj and the other with someone called Arifaj Madjun. I want to ask you about both of those? First of all, Shaban Sadikaj. You told us in your evidence that you had a conversation with him in September. You said it was at the beginning of September. Can you be any more specific about the date?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. Probably early September but I'm not positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: See if can date it a little bit more accurately. By the time you had the conversation with Shaban Sadikaj, had you already learned about the discovery of what was then thought to be your father's body in the Lake Radonjic Canal? Did you already know about that when you spoke to Shaban Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You went to Hotel Pastrik at one point to identify some clothing, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We did go but nothing was known at that time, and I don't remember the date we went. It wasn't until later that they eventually told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We have records of the dates that you went, Mr. Vlahovic, so don't worry about that. You were there when clothing was identified that was thought to belong to your father, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was the conversation with Shaban Sadikaj before or after that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you spoke to Shaban Sadikaj at his home, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it on the road near his home?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He lived in Dashinoc. Were you in Dashinoc when you had this conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: What were you doing in Dashinoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to go and see him. I wanted to go and see Djevdet. He had told Milojka that he should throw both his parents out, as well as Milica.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you went there specifically to speak to Shaban, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not Shaban, Djevdet.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. You went to speak to Djevdet; yes?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: At that time did you think Djevdet had been a KLA leader in Dashinoc?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you go there once or more than once, to Dashinoc, in September?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once, just that once, in Ratis and in Dashinoc. I didn't go twice. I didn't go many times. I just went that once.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And on that same occasion, you went both to Ratishe and to Dashinoc; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I first went to that house. It's not too far from our house, from our house to Dasinovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And so does it follow that the conversation that you had with Arifaj Madjun was on the same day as the conversation that you had with Shaban Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with Madjun in Ratis.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it on the same day that you spoke to Shaban Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's a different village, and this is yet a different one. It could not have been on the same day. I had spoken to Madjun earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you spoke to Madjun first before you spoke to Shaban; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Mr. Vlahovic, were you aware when you went to Dashinoc that there were international monitors operating in the area, international people looking at what had taken place there? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know that there were monitors all over the place. I didn't know about Dasinovac specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Stanisa Radosevic has given evidence to this Tribunal that when he went to Dashinoc on about the 9th or 10th of September, the majority of the houses had been set fire to and some were still on fire. Did you see houses that had been damaged by fire when you went to Dashinoc and spoke to Shaban Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So when you were there, there was no evidence of damage by fire to the houses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. I want to go through what you say Shaban Sadikaj told you. As far as your parents were concerned, you told us yesterday that Shaban Sadikaj told you that your parents had stayed in their own house for 10 to 15 days after the date on which you had last seen them, the 20th of April; you told us that Miloica Radunovic, the wife of Milos Radunovic, had stayed with them, according to Shaban Sadikaj; and you told us that he told you that a neighbour called Syle Kuci could have helped them get out but didn't; and you told us that he didn't tell you anything else about your parents other than that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also said about Milica that she had been over to ask about Milos, to talk to his cousin, but she didn't know that they had killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to come to that in a moment. Now, you told us yesterday afternoon that in addition to what he told you about your parents, Shaban Sadikaj had also told you about something that had happened to Slobodan Radosevic and Milos Radunovic. You said that he told you that a meeting had been held in the house of Djevdet Sadikaj, the son of Shaban; you said that Shaban told you that he had seen the people at the meeting arresting Milos Radunovic when he was on his way to Slobodan Radosevic's house; and you said that he told you that he tried to intervene to prevent that, but that they shouted at him and chased him back to his home; and all of that, you said, he told you had happened within a few days of the date that you last saw your father. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he told me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, when you made your statement to the Prosecution investigator in April 2002, you didn't mention anything at all about what you now say Shaban Sadikaj told you about the alleged abduction of Milos Radunovic, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, we have your statement available, and, if needs be, we can put it up on the screen, but I'll just read to you -- I'll just read to you the passage in which you described the conversation with Shaban Sadikaj, and this is the only reference to it. "After the Yugoslav army and the MUP had taken control of the area around my village in September 1998, I travelled to Dasinovac. I spoke with Shaban Sadikaj whose son Djevdet was probably the top KLA commander in Dasinovac. According to Shaban, his son and Rustem Sadrijaj or Kamisi, I'm not sure of the family name, and the third man were the main KLA men in Dasinovac, and they had perpetrated many horrible crimes. Shaban also related to me that my parents had stayed in their house for 10 to 15 days after the road had been blocked and that Milica Radunovic had stayed with them. During this time she did not know what had happened to her husband. Shaban told me that my parents' neighbour Syle Kuci could have assisted to escape but he chose not to." That is all that is recorded in your statement about that conversation. There's no reference at all to the alleged abduction of Milos Radunovic. Now, Mr. Vlahovic, why did you not mention then what you're telling the Tribunal now about that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did say then. I must have because that's what had happened. I don't think I would have just skipped it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vlahovic, at the end of that interview in April 2002, this statement was read over to you, wasn't it, in a language that you understood by an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I thought that I'd stated that for the record. But that's what had happened and there's nothing that can change that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, it's perfectly clear to all of us who have your statement in front of us, Mr. Vlahovic, that there is nothing recorded in it to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. There is nothing. But that's what happened, so there you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Stanisa Radosevic has told us about a conversation he had with an Albanian man in Dashinoc at about this time. Was he present when you spoke to Shaban Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was anybody that you knew, any Serbs that you knew, in Dashinoc at the time that you went there?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you this, Mr. Vlahovic: Did you see a Mercedes car outside Mr. Sadikaj's house?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see a smashed-up Mercedes, white, 123, one of ours, and a black cow, too, one of ours again.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Whose Mercedes was it you say you saw outside the Sadikaj house?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Belonged to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to us, our family. And the cow, too, the black one.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Were you angry to see your car parked outside the Sadikaj's house? Did you think they'd stolen it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I asked Shaban, and he said the car belonged to Djevdet and Rustem.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You knew that wasn't true, Mr. Vlahovic. It was your car, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our car but no longer. Anyone could have had it. They had killed my parents. What could have stopped them from taking my car, given the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I repeat my question: Did it make you angry to see that they had stolen your car, as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I was angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you were, Mr. Vlahovic, because I suggest that you weren't there alone, you were there with a number of others, and that together you beat Shaban Sadikaj. That's the truth about this encounter, isn't it, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That is not the truth. That is not the truth at all. None of it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we please see Defence document identification 1D11-0048 [Realtime transcript read in error "1D11-0488"] please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. It needs a number, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, please. Marked for identification, and I will be asking for it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number D15, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If we can just look at the first page, first of all. 0048; yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, this, Mr. Vlahovic, I'm not expecting you to understand it because it's in English only, but I shall read you the passage I want to take your attention to. But so you understand what you're looking at, this is an investigator's report from a Prosecution investigator who went to speak to Shaban Sadikaj about your meeting with him, okay? You understand what it is we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can we turn to pages 5 and 6; 5, first of all, briefly. That's 4, I think. That's 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, in the statement of Miloica Vlahovic, there is a paragraph where he talks about a man called Shaban Sadikaj from Dasinovac. This paragraph mentions Djevdet Sadikaj as the main KLA commander in Dasinovac. It also states that: "Miloica Vlahovic spoke to Shaban Sadikaj who told him that Miloica's parents had stayed in his house for 10 to 15 days and that Milica Radunovic was with them." Now, I just want to be clear. There's obviously been a misunderstanding by the investigator because your witness statement said that Shaban Sadikaj had told you that your parents had stayed in their house for 10 or 15 days, and it's obvious that the investigator had thought that what you were saying was that Shaban Sadikaj had said that your parents had stayed at the Sadikaj's house for 10 or 15 days, but you never told anybody that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So now if we look over to page 6, we'll just go through it and I'll read it to you and I hope at a translatable speed? "OL," that's the investigator, "visited Dashinoc on the 19th of November, 2005. Dashinoc is a very small and remote village. Shaban Sadikaj's house was found and his daughter, Minire Sadikaj opened the door. One of the sons came to the door and did not seem friendly. The investigator asked him whether Shaban Sadikaj was at home and he said that he was. He wanted to know what it was about and OL asked to come inside to explain. They turned out to be another brother present. Also their paralysed mother and some other children were in the room. "The sons did most of the talking. The investigator explained that the interest was to speak about some things that happened during the war. The brothers had a very angry attitude and said that the wrong persons are being indicted for war crimes. One of them mentioned Rade Vlahovic as someone who had committed a lot of crimes." That would be a reference to your brother, would it, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it's true or not is a different kettle of fish altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "The investigator didn't mention what his actual interest was about, but asked if it was possible to speak to the father. They said he always gets very upset when he talks about the war because of what the Serbs did to him, but it was okay to try and talk to him. He came to the room after a while. Shaban Sadikaj is 74 and is not in a state of mental health to be interviewed properly. He didn't listen to any questions and he kept talking about when the Serbs came and took him at gunpoint. They said that they were going to kill him and they beat him up badly and he lost his conscious. When he woke up, some Albanians, who had passed by, had managed to save him from being killed. "Shaban Sadikaj kept going in and out of the room and telling the same story. "The brothers said that the incident with Shaban Sadikaj happened in September 1998. Everyone else had already left the village, but the father stayed behind. "The investigator asked the brothers about the KLA in Dashinoc. They said that they had their own village defence and people defended their own compounds. They felt like part of the KLA, but they were not under the command of Ramush or Tahir." The investigator notes that he had visited the village earlier and met some of the other Sadikajs who had said the same basic thing, leaving themselves outside any actual command. It goes on: "Dashinoc is a small village and according to the brothers, all of the 15 houses these days are related and called Sadikaj. Serbs used to live in the village and everyone got on well until the war. When asked about the Vlahovic family, they said that they used to be good friends, but it changed all of a sudden. They mentioned that even during the beginning of the war, they used to help anyone who was in need, no matter what ethnicity. "The brothers would not give a clear answer as to who was the main commander of the army in the village. They said everyone took care of their own bit. Also, they claim again that they weren't affected by the troops of Ramush or Tahir. They don't mention anything else about RH, but they were very upset with what the Serbs did. They say that their houses were destroyed and their relatives were killed by people who used to be their friends." Now, Mr. Vlahovic, when you saw Shaban Sadikaj, had he already been beaten, as far as you could see? Mr. Vlahovic? When you saw Shaban Sadikaj, had he already been beaten, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they say in this statement that they were helping the Serbs. What Serbs? There were no Serbs around during the war. It was back in 1998. They were killing the Serbs. Nobody got out of Dasinovac alive. None of this is true at all. How could they have helped any Serbs at all? So it's not true. And secondly --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could you just answer my question, Mr. Vlahovic, without telling us about the Serbs for a moment. Was he already beaten when you spoke to him or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I spoke to him, he had not yet been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Did you know about him being beaten afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't see him afterwards. I didn't hear from him. When I did see him, he seemed "business as usual" and in good health, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Because do you know, Mr. Vlahovic, who Salih Sadikaj is?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You are recorded in a complaint together with your brother Novak and your brother Goran and Stanisa Radosevic, your friend, as having beaten Shaban Sadikaj brutally for about half an hour with pistols, machine-guns, and knives. Did you do that, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who could possibly have survived that sort of thing, what they're saying here. Who could have survived? As I said a while ago, I was alone. Shaban was fine. I didn't touch him or anything at all. We just spoke. And that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you take your pistol with you when you went? The pistol you had, did you take it with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because one of the things he's recorded as being beaten with is a pistol; a pistol-whipping, in other words. Did you do that, Mr. Vlahovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I repeat: I didn't even touch him, let alone pistol-whip him, as you suggest. This is a lie. What it says here is a lie. And secondly, I was on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him, I spoke to him, and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you know who Halil Sadikaj is?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halil?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He know who you are, Mr. Vlahovic. Is it your evidence that you're on good terms with these people, with Salih Sadikaj, the man who I just mentioned to you? Is it your evidence that you were on good terms with him by September 1998? They were your friends?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: September 1998, there was no relationship at all. I saw Shaban then and I never saw them again, not before April. Not since April 1998. I didn't see any of the Sadikajs. The only one I saw was Shaban.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me make my question clear to you, Mr. Vlahovic. You've told us that you got on well with your Albanian neighbours, haven't you, until April --

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you described Shaban Sadikaj as a friend of yours, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that Shaban Sadikaj was a friend of mine. I never said that. I said that we didn't have any dispute with anyone. We were on good terms with everyone. But I never mentioned Shaban specifically, and I never said that we were friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So there was no problem between your family and his?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason why Salih Sadikaj should make up -- MR. DI FAZIO: I object to that question. Mr. Emmerson should know better. That is calling for the most rampant speculations. In fact, he said -- he said he didn't even know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He said he didn't know Halil Sadikaj, thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Whether he did or didn't, it's a question that Mr. Emmerson should know better not to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't accept the criticism at all. This witness has given evidence that they were on good terms. I'm asking whether there's anything in their relationship which could cause this person concerned to have a motive to fabricate an account of a beating of his father. MR. DI FAZIO: No, the question is: Can you think of any reason why Salih Sadikaj should make up," and we know what was coming after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's exactly the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand now that it's the formulation, rather than the content of the question that bothers you, Mr. Di Fazio. I, by the way, urge both parties to use the language which does not make problems any bigger than they are already, that this rampant or speculation is -- speculation, as such, should not be sought. Could you formulate the question in such a way that Mr. Di Fazio is -- would take into account what Mr. Di Fazio brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, do you know of any reason in your relationship, that is, the relationship between your family and Mr. Sadikaj's, which could cause someone to have a sufficient grudge against your family to make up a false allegation that you and your brothers beat Shaban Sadikaj?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had been such good friends they would have got my father and mother out. They were an old couple who didn't harm anyone, and that is why they made up the whole story. And I stand by it 1.000 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. And finally on this topic, I've got one more area to cover, but finally on this topic, Mr. Vlahovic, a man called Halil Sadikaj has lodged a complaint that together with your brothers Novak and Goran and together with Stanisa Radosevic, Novak Stijovic and your cousin Zvonko Markovic, you took part in looting the Albanian houses on the 7th of September. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a lie. I'm telling you again, it's completely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The allegation is that together you entered Albanian houses and robbed them of electrical equipment and cars. Did you take a car, Mr. Vlahovic? Did you take your car? MR. DI FAZIO: I object to that question, if Your Honours please. Mr. Emmerson -- I wonder if Mr. Emmerson is listening to the answers. Mr. Emmerson quite rightly put to the witness that this man has made a -- what he called, lodged a complaint against the brothers, and then asked him -- and that this man had taken part in looting, and very rightly asked him, is that true? And then the witness said: "That's a lie. I'm telling you again, it's completely impossible." Next question, into the details of the looting. Now, the witness has said he hasn't done it. That's the end of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, it's not. MR. DI FAZIO: If Mr. Emmerson wants to put documents to him or other matters, then so be it. But once the witness has said no, it didn't happen, how much further can he take it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Di Fazio, I think that in cross-examination, that a first "no" would not prevent cross-examining counsel from putting any further questions. Let me just give you an example. No, I'll not do that at this moment. So, therefore, within certain limits --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I won't press beyond one further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Within certain limits if there is a denial of a general nature, then it is not per se impermissible to put an additional question introducing a certain detail which might refresh the memory of the witness or might be making him aware that certain details seem to be known by the cross-examining party. There are certainly limits to that; I fully agree with that. But that limit has not been reached yet. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I am aware of techniques in cross-examination. Sometimes the tone becomes a bit more intense than at other moments. I am inviting the parties to keep that within limits themselves; otherwise, I'll have to draw the lines. If you keep within the limits, I don't have to draw the lines; if you go clearly beyond what the limits should be, then I have to intervene. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Entirely understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The car, your car, did you take it away with you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And what you said a minute ago is absolutely untrue. Not a single word is true. There was no looting. It's -- it's fantasy.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Do you say there was no looting or are you saying you didn't take part in it? Are you giving evidence that the Albanian houses were not looted in Dashinoc in September 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that I didn't even see them being looted, let alone myself being involved in that. That's a complete fabrication. It's just a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I see. Can I move on now to the final main topic I want to cover which is the conversation you say you had with Arifaj Madjun. Now, you told us yesterday that in September you met Arifaj Madjun and he told you that he had seen your parents and Milica Radunovic being taken away towards Gllogjan. Now, you said yesterday that he told you that the men were armed and in uniform but that he didn't know them, and you said that he didn't give you any description of the uniforms they were wearing and you didn't ask him, and that he didn't tell you their ethnicity and you didn't ask him that either? Now, against that background, I just want to ask you one or two further questions. The record of your videolink interview from Belgrade on the 8th of March has a passage which reads as follows: "The witness," that is you, "did not ask when this had happened and Madjun didn't say anything about the date." Was that an accurate record of what you said in the proofing session when you spoke on the videolink from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't ask him when they were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So as far as you knew from the information he'd supplied you with, it could have happened, this incident, at any time between the 20th of September -- the 20th of April and the beginning of September? You have absolutely no idea when during those months it happened and you didn't think to ask; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him when this happened precisely, but it must have happened much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, didn't you want to know when it had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nuo went. They were not at home, so that was more or less the period of time when this incident happened. If they weren't at home two weeks later, after the 20th of April, it must have been early May, so I did -- there was no need for me to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This was the Nuo who you told us earlier on had told Rade that your parents were released at Prilep? Is that the person we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said yesterday that Madjun told you that someone called Bajram Imer had told these men not to touch your parents, had told them that they were elderly and that they should be released, and that these armed men then tried to kill Bajram Imer for intervening. Is that what you say Arifaj Madjun told you?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he told me then was, there was no way for us to save them, and he added that Imer Ademi, I think, was his last name, insisted vehemently that they be released and that they wanted to kill him for that, that's what he said; that he couldn't save them.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did Arifaj Madjun say how they tried to kill him, or what he had done to escape from being killed? Did he give you that part of the incident or not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him at the time what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you try and speak to Bajram Imer or Imer Ademi yourself? Try to find him and speak to him yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't look for him and I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you suggest to any of your three brothers in the police that they should try and find this man who saw your parents being taken away?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because as far as we understand it, after your conversation with Arifaj Madjun, you didn't know who these men were, you had no identification for them, and you didn't know when this incident had happened. Didn't you want to know who it was that had taken your parents away, get their identities from the man who was an eye-witness to it, see if he knew who they were?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the identity, I knew that they were Albanians. There was no other people; there were only Albanians. And everybody knew who was in command in Gllogjan. Madjun didn't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Didn't you want to find out from Bajram Imer whether he knew who these particular men were who had taken your parents away?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Madjun didn't know and they were neighbours, if this one didn't know him and they were neighbours, then the other one didn't know them either. That was common knowledge. I knew that they had been taken to Glodjane. There was no need for me to ask. And everybody knew who was living there; the Albanians were living there. And everybody knew who was in charge. It was common knowledge. Everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll come to that in just a second. Did Madjun tell you whether these men were in a car or on foot?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him at the time. I didn't need that information. I thought it was irrelevant, whether they were in a vehicle or on foot. My main concern and worry was that they had been taken away. That's why I didn't ask him about this specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Forgive me for putting this to you, Mr. Vlahovic, but the description that you're giving us of a conversation with a man you say told you he'd seen your parents being taken away in which you didn't ask for the ethnicity of the men or a description of their uniforms or the date when it happened, and you didn't go and look for another witness to see if they could help you with this information, I'm going to suggest to you that you are not telling the truth about this and that had you had such a conversation, you would have been asking and seeking far greater information about the circumstances that this man was describing to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have this conversation, definitely. Why should I invent that, according to you? But I also knew that they were not at home two weeks later. I knew that there were no Serbs there. The Serbs had all been killed. I know that only Siptars were living there. I know that the HQ was in Glodjane, and that the man in charge was Ramush Haradinaj. So I knew all that. Why should I be going around asking people questions? And the only time when I was able to go there was in September, when everything was over already and it was known for a fact that they were not alive any longer. That is all true. These are your speculations and your guesswork, and it's up to you to think that. But that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, fifteen minutes ago, you said you had one topic to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And earlier -- yes, I do understand. Earlier you said whether we'd allow you to use one hour. It's now 75 minutes. How much time would you need? Because I'm thinking about the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can certainly finish in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make it seven, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The location where Madjun told you that he had seen this take place, you told us it was on a bridge crossing the Ratiska River; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he tell you which direction they took from there?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This road leads only to Rznic and Glodjane, nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it leads from Ratishe across the bridge towards Irzniq, and at Irzniq you can go -- excuse me, at Irzniq, you can go left to Gllogjan, straight ahead towards Prilep, or right towards Pozar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an intersection; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And so when you tell us that they were taken towards Gllogjan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we get in any further troubles, let's verify. Mr. Vlahovic, is it correct that the bridge you're talking about is the bridge near Rznic? Because you suggest -- it's an implicit suggestion, your question, that they took the route west and then -- or then I have misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's not a suggestion; it was a question. I'm asking the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's try to deal with the question in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that we give the witness an opportunity to say whether he went south or east or west --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at the beginning, because there are several routes to the road, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm obviously trying to do it as quickly as possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- without taking the witness to the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But let's be clear, Mr. Vlahovic. The bridge that you describe is on a road that leads from Gornji Ratishe to Irzniq, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether they were going east towards Gornji Ratishe or west towards Irzniq? Did he say that one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Rznic, that they were headed towards Rznic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So he said that without telling you whether they were on foot or in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't mention that. He just told me that they had been taken in the direction of Rznic. Whether they were in a car or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And had they reached Rznic, they could then have gone straight ahead towards Prilep, left towards Gllogjan, or right towards Pozar and Kordolija, could they not?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have gone had they been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And had they gone towards Prilep, they would have been alive now. So the only direction they could have been taken was towards Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is your inference, Mr. Vlahovic, isn't it? You weren't told by Madjun -- excuse me. You were not told by Madjun, were you, that he heard these men saying they were going to Gllogjan?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him that, but had they gone towards Prilep, they would have gotten out, they would have been alive. Where else could have they gone?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Don't, please, speculate about where they might have gone. This man did not tell you that he had heard anyone saying they were going towards Gllogjan, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILOICA VLAHOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. But the location where my mother was later found confirmed that. She was found in the canal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vlahovic, it's relatively simple. What Mr. Emmerson seeks to find out is whether you made the inference that they could not have been heading -- is there a translation problem? I'll try it again. Mr. Emmerson tries to find out whether it's because you think that they could not have been heading to any other place in view of what you later learned, to any other place than Gllogjan, or whether in your conversation you were told that someone during that encounter said to Madjun, that because of that they could have only been heading to Gllogjan. So was it said, or is it just because you can't imagine anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say yes, you mean that you can't imagine anything else, but that it was not explicitly said? Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I cannot imagine anything other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it was not explicitly -- you were not told that this was explicitly said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And finally this, if I may. You mentioned your mother in the canal.
